'''Julian Thomas Pierce''' (January 2, 1946 – March 25/26, 1988) was an American lawyer and [[Lumbee]] activist. Born in [[Hoke County, North Carolina]], he became the first person in his family to go to college and worked for several years as a chemist at shipyards in Virginia before obtaining his [[Juris Doctor]] degree. Following two years of work for the [[United States Securities and Exchange Commission|U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission]], he moved to [[Robeson County, North Carolina]] to direct a [[legal aid]] organization and in that capacity co-authored a petition to the federal government asking for the extension of federal recognition to the Lumbee tribe. In 1988 he resigned from his job to pursue a candidacy for a new [[North Carolina Superior Court|Superior Court]] judgeship. Running against the local district attorney and over the objections of the county sheriff, he was found murdered in his home several weeks before the primary election. While his murder was officially determined to be the result of an interpersonal dispute, the circumstances of his death remain unclear, with his friends and family having advanced suspicions that he was assassinated for political reasons.

==Early life==

Julian Pierce was born in [[Hoke County, North Carolina]], on January 2, 1946, to John S. Pierce and Mary J. Pierce.<ref name= sketch>{{cite news| title = Julian Pierce: A Biographical Sketch| newspaper = The Carolina Indian Voice| page = 6| date = November 2, 1978| url = https://newspapers.digitalnc.org/lccn/sn83008090/1978-11-02/ed-1/seq-6}}</ref> The Pierces were  [[Lumbee people|Lumbee Indian]] tenant farmers who had moved to the Hoke Indian community of Hawkeye from [[Chesterfield County, South Carolina]].<ref name="findagrave">{{cite web |title=John Sampson Pierce (1904-1967) |url=https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/107383502/john_sampson-pierce |website=www.findagrave.com |publisher=Findagrave |access-date=19 August 2026 |language=en}}</ref> Julian was one of 13 children.{{sfn|Lowery|2018|p=189}} He attended Antioch Elementary School and then Hawkeye Elementary and High School, from which he graduated in 1962 at the age of 16. He then attended [[University of North Carolina at Pembroke|Pembroke State College]] in [[Pembroke, North Carolina]], graduating with a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in [[Chemistry]] in 1966.<ref name= sketch/> He was the first person in his family to obtain a college degree.<ref name= scholarship>{{cite news| title = Julian Pierce Law Scholarship established at NC Central University| newspaper = The Carolina Indian Voice| page = 1| volume = 31 | issue = 46| date = November 13, 2003| url = https://newspapers.digitalnc.org/lccn/sn83008090/2003-11-13/ed-1/seq-1}}</ref> He married and had three children,<ref name= sketch/> but eventually separated from his wife.<ref name= haimes/>

==Career==
=== Early activities ===
After graduating from Pembroke State College, Pierce became a [[chemist]] for the [[Northrop Grumman Newport News|Newport News Shipbuilding]] and Dry Dock Company in [[Newport News, Virginia]]. There he worked on chemical instruments, quality control testing, and [[decontamination|decontaminating]] [[Nuclear reactor technology|nuclear reactors]]. In 1969, he became a chemist in the [[U.S. Navy]] Shipyard in [[Norfolk, Virginia]], where he performed similar work.<ref name= sketch/> In 1973, Pierce moved back to North Carolina and enrolled at the [[North Carolina Central University School of Law]].<ref name= haag/> After graduating from law school in 1976, he became an attorney for the [[United States Securities and Exchange Commission|U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission]]'s office of general counsel in [[Washington, D.C.]] In that capacity, he mostly compiled [[Brief (law)|briefs]] on the commission's behalf, though he also occasionally represented it in court.<ref name= sketch/> While working there, Pierce attended [[Georgetown University Law Center|Georgetown School of Law]] to earn his [[Master of Laws]] in [[Tax]]ation.<ref name=Julian />

=== Legal defense and Lumbee recognition ===
In 1978, Pierce moved to [[Robeson County]] to become the first director of Lumbee River Legal Services, a new [[Legal aid in the United States|legal aid]] organization headquartered in Pembroke and designed to serve the poor in Robeson and four surrounding counties.<ref name= haag>{{cite news| last1 = Haag| first1 = Rich| last2 = Greyard| first2 = Harry | title = Slain Lumbee Activist Began Legal Aid Agency| newspaper = The Charlotte Observer| page = 1C| date = March 27, 1988| url = https://www.newspapers.com/clip/112330188/the-charlotte-observer/}}</ref>{{sfn|Blu|2001|p=259}} He worked in that capacity for ten years.<ref name=Julian /> In 1981, he served as counsel for residents suing the [[Lumberton, North Carolina|Lumberton]] City School Board, arguing that the system's annexations of mostly-white jurisdictions in the county in the 1960s violated the [[Voting Rights Act of 1965]]. The [[United States District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina]] ultimately ruled that the city board had to seek clearance of its action from the [[U.S. Department of Justice]].<ref>{{cite news| last = Barton| first = Bruce| title = Lumberton City Schools Expected To Lose In Federal Court| newspaper = The Carolina Indian Voice| page = 1| volume = 9| issue = 40| date = October 1, 1981| url = https://newspapers.digitalnc.org/lccn/sn83008090/1981-10-01/ed-1/seq-1/}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| last = Barton| first = Bruce| title = Lumberton City Schools Found "In Violation" of 1965 Voting Rights Act| newspaper = The Carolina Indian Voice| page = 1| volume = 9 | issue = 42| date = October 22, 1981| url = https://newspapers.digitalnc.org/lccn/sn83008090/1981-10-22/ed-1/seq-1}}</ref>

Pierce also heavily studied laws concerning [[Tribal sovereignty in the United States|federal recognition of Native American tribes]].{{sfn|Lowery|2018|p=189}} The Lumbee were the largest group of resident Native Americans in the United States east of the [[Mississippi River]]. While they had been recognized by North Carolina's state government as tribal community since the 1880s, they never achieved complete federal recognition.{{sfn|Lowery|2018|pp=1, 9–10}} In 1987 Pierce and three others co-authored a petition on behalf of Lumbee River Legal Services and the [[Lumbee Regional Development Association]] to request that the [[United States Department of the Interior]] grant federal recognition of the Lumbee people as a tribe.<ref name=Julian />{{sfn|Blu|2001|pp=254, 256}} The petition was denied due to language in the Lumbee Act of 1956. The petitioners then proposed a recognition bill for [[United States Congress|Congress]] to adopt, but it failed due to opposition from the Department of the Interior and from other recognized tribes.<ref name=Julian />

=== Judicial candidacy ===
In 1987, the [[North Carolina General Assembly]] created nine new [[North Carolina Superior Court|Superior Court]] judgeships, including one covering Robeson County with the goal of allowing minority candidates better odds of winning judicial office. [[Joe Freeman Britt]], the county's white district attorney, declared himself a candidate for the office in the 1988 [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] primary. Britt was known for pushing for death sentences in criminal trials. No [[Republican Party (United States)|Republicans]] entered the contest.<ref name= wildman>{{cite news| last = Wildman| first = John| title = Controversial Britt Known As Tough| newspaper = The Charlotte Observer| page = 12A| date = April 3, 1988| url = https://www.newspapers.com/clip/112357040/controversial-britt/}}</ref> Pierce announced in January 1988 that he would run against Britt in the primary, making him the first person to ever challenge the district attorney in an electoral contest. He resigned from his position at Lumber River Legal Services and organized a campaign, pledging to be a "hard but fair judge".{{sfn|Lowery|2018|p=190}} He also indicated that he would investigate allegations that Sheriff [[Hubert Stone]] was engaged in a protection racket with drug dealers and that Britt had engaged in prosecutorial abuses.{{sfn|Lowery|2018|p=190}} Stone tried to convince Pierce to drop out of the contest.{{sfn|Lowery|2018|p=191}} He said in a 1989 interview, "I approached him and asked him not to run for Superior Court Judge, and asked him to run for [a lesser office]. I said, 'Joe Freeman Britt is going to run, and I'd rather not have a fight in an election over it.'"<ref name= haimes/> Pierce refused, and over the course of February and March, it was alleged that Stone attempted to employ bribery and blackmail against Pierce.{{sfn|Lowery|2018|p=191}}

Pierce's campaign workers feared for his safety. At a political dinner on March 24, 1988, Stone took Pierce aside to discuss the campaign. According to Stone, "[Pierce] said, 'I know you and Joe [Freeman Britt] are working on me.' And I said, 'I'm not going to hurt you.'"<ref name= haimes>{{cite news| last = Haimes| first = Nicole Lucas| title = Who killed Julian Pierce?| newspaper = [[MEL Magazine]]| date = 2017| url = https://melmagazine.com/en-us/story/who-killed-julian-pierce| access-date = March 9, 2021}}</ref> Pierce was reportedly angered by the encounter and stated that from then on he would focus on mobilizing black and Indian voters. The following day, a campaign worker told him that sheriff's deputies were spying on him and his campaign manager urged him to retain a bodyguard. Pierce declined to do so, explaining, "If it happens then it happens—they can kill me but they can't eat me."{{sfn|Lowery|2018|p=191}}

==Murder==
On the morning of March 26, 1988, just a few weeks before the election, Pierce's body was found in his home in [[Wakulla, North Carolina|Wakulla]] by his cousins with [[shotgun]] wounds to his head, chest, and stomach. Police, including state investigators and Stone, came to Pierce's home to investigate the murder.<ref name= haimes/>{{sfn|Lowery|2018|pp=191, 193}} There were no signs of forced entry or theft.{{sfn|Lowery|2018|p=191}} A crowd of approximately 200 Lumbee gathered at the scene and Stone asked for their help in providing information about the killing. He also told a reporter that the killing appeared to be a political assassination. A few days later, he announced that investigators had concluded that Pierce was killed by Johnny Goins with the assistance of Sandy Chavis. According to Stone, Goins shot Pierce because Pierce's girlfriend had told Goins to stay away from her daughter whom Goins had previously dated. Goins' blood and fingerprints were found at Pierce's home. Chavis was arrested and charged with murder, while Goins was found dead from an apparently self-inflicted shotgun wound to the head in his father's house. Investigators quickly declared Goins' death a suicide, and Stone said he had probably killed himself to avoid being arrested, re-iterating that Pierce's murder was due to a personal dispute and not political.<ref name= haimes/>

Pierce's family and many members of the Lumbee community doubted the investigators' conclusions.<ref name= haimes/> Pierce's briefcase, which had reportedly contained documents corroborating corruption claims in county government, had gone missing, as had the sheriff's office dispatch tapes from the night of March 25/26. Goins' autopsy mentioned that he had written a confessional suicide note, but law enforcement officials never produced it. A bloody footprint found in Pierce's house did not match Goins or Chavis.<ref name= haimes/> As for Goins, the state medical examiner and state investigators disagreed on whether he shot himself through the mouth or the side of the head. No gunshot residue was found on his hands and the autopsy did not conclude that he had fired the gun himself.{{sfn|Lowery|2018|p=193}} A crime scene photo also showed that the shotgun used to shoot Goins was laying in his lap with its [[breechloader|breech]] open. When asked about this in 1989, Stone maintained that the shotgun was found with its breech closed. When asked if he thought Goins killed Pierce, Stone refused to comment, citing Chavis' impending trial. In 1990 Chavis' murder trial was canceled after key witnesses for the prosecution refused to testify, and Chavis entered an [[Alford plea]] to accessory to murder after the fact.<ref name= haimes/> Circumstances surrounding the murder of Pierce remain contested, and members of his family and elected officials have in the years since his death questioned the investigation.{{sfn|Lowery|2018|pp=192–193}}<ref name= haimes/>

== Legacy ==
Pierce was buried in Hoke County near his parents' graves. A funeral for him was held at Pembroke State University and attended by 1,700 people, including the governor, the chief justice of the [[North Carolina State Supreme Court]], and several other state officials.{{sfn|Lowery|2018|p=193}} In the aftermath of the murder, a local civil rights march in Lumberton scheduled for April 4 to commemorate the [[Assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.|assassination of]] [[Martin Luther King Jr.]] was reoriented around honoring Pierce.<ref>{{cite news| last = Johnston| first = Erica| title = March planned for King becomes Pierce memorial| newspaper = Winston-Salem Chronicle| agency = Associated Press| page = A1| volume = XIV| issue = 33 | date = April 7, 1988| url = https://newspapers.digitalnc.org/lccn/sn85042324/1988-04-07/ed-1/seq-1}}</ref> Speakers at the event encouraged attendees to vote for Pierce in the judgeship election despite his death.<ref>{{cite news| last = Ellis| first = Tezra| title = Student attends Robeson march| newspaper = Winston-Salem Chronicle| page = A13| volume = XIV| issue = 33 | date = April 7, 1988| url = https://newspapers.digitalnc.org/lccn/sn85042324/1988-04-07/ed-1/seq-13}}</ref> Britt was automatically declared the winner of the [[Partisan primary|primary election]]. However, some reporters and campaign workers counted the votes and determined that Pierce actually won the vote posthumously, 10,787 to 8,231.<ref name=Julian>{{cite news|last=Pierce|first=Julia|title=Julian Pierce '76 : An attorney who was "for the people" |url=http://www.nccu.edu/law/alumni/2003OfCounsel.pdf |access-date=May 31, 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040407115048/http://www.nccu.edu/law/alumni/2003OfCounsel.pdf |archive-date=April 7, 2004|date=2004|newspaper=Of Counsel|publisher=North Carolina Central University|pages=2–3}}</ref> To bring more racial balance to the court system, the General Assembly created another judgeship in the county and the governor appointed Lumbee attorney Dexter Brooks, a friend of Pierce, to the post.{{sfn|Lowery|2018|p=194}}<ref>{{cite news| title = Julian Pierce & Judge Dexter Brooks Senior Resident Superior Court Judge featured in the North Carolina Bar Association's Centennial Exhibit Posters| newspaper = The Carolina Indian Voice | page = 3| volume = 27| issue = 25| date = June 22, 2000| url = https://newspapers.digitalnc.org/lccn/sn83008090/2000-06-22/ed-1/seq-3/}}</ref>

Lumbee River Legal Services posthumously dedicated its law library room to Pierce and commissioned a portrait of him to be hung there.<ref>{{cite news| title = Lumbee River Legal Services Observes Tenth Anniversary| newspaper = The Carolina Indian Voice| page = 1| volume = 16| issue = 45| date = November 10, 1988| url = https://newspapers.digitalnc.org/lccn/sn83008090/1988-11-10/ed-1/seq-1/}}</ref> A scholarship for law students at North Carolina Central University was established in Pierce's honor in 2003.<ref name= scholarship/> That year the [[National Legal Aid & Defender Association]] created the Pierce-Hickerson Award in honor of Pierce and Robert Hickerson to be given to lawyers who perform excellent legal work on behalf of Native Americans.<ref>{{cite web| url = https://www.nlada.org/about-nlada/awards| title = Equal Justice Awards| publisher = National Legal Aid & Defender Association| access-date = November 1, 2022}}</ref>  In June 2015, the [[North Carolina House of Representatives]] passed a unanimous resolution in commemoration of Pierce.<ref>{{cite news| title = General Assembly honors Julian Pierce with resolution| newspaper = The Robesonian| date = June 26, 2015| url = https://www.robesonian.com/news/business/628/general-assembly-honorsjulian-pierce-with-resolution| access-date = November 1, 2022}}</ref>
